subject: ela
description: Students delineate and evaluate the argument a speaker makes in a spoken presentation such as a speech, oral report, debate turn, podcast segment, classroom presentation, or announcement. They first identify the speaker's overall position or central claim, then trace the specific claims the speaker advances to support it. For each claim they decide whether the speaker backs it with reasons and evidence (facts, examples, data, expert testimony, logical reasoning) or whether the claim is left unsupported, resting on opinion, bias, emotional appeal, repetition, or bare assertion. Students distinguish a reason (the why behind a claim) from evidence (the concrete proof), and they judge how relevant and sufficient that support is. Because the standard concerns listening, every item embeds the speaker's words as a transcript or script of what was said, so the student needs nothing external to answer. The student reads the transcript as if hearing the speaker and evaluates the spoken argument it represents.
subSkills: Identify the speaker's overall argument or central position in a spoken presentation
Delineate the specific claims the speaker makes to advance that argument, in the order they are presented
Distinguish a claim (a statement the speaker wants the listener to accept) from a reason or a piece of evidence the speaker offers
Distinguish a reason (the logic for why a claim is true) from evidence (the concrete facts, examples, or data that prove it)
Determine whether a given claim is supported by reasons and evidence or is left unsupported
Match a specific claim to the reason or evidence the speaker provides for it
Evaluate the quality of the support: judge whether the evidence is relevant to the claim and whether there is enough of it
Recognize unsupported moves in spoken argument such as opinion stated as fact, emotional appeal, biased or loaded wording, repetition, or sweeping generalization that lacks proof

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the speaker's central argument
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript of the speaker's remarks embedded in the item, then state the speaker's overall position: 'What is the main argument the speaker makes in this speech?' The answer names the position the speaker wants the audience to accept, not just the topic the speech is about.

problemArchetypes.name: Delineate a specific claim
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then pick out one of the speaker's claims: 'Which statement is a claim the speaker is trying to prove?' The answer points to a statement the speaker wants accepted, as opposed to a neutral fact or a piece of supporting evidence.

problemArchetypes.name: Distinguish claim from reason from evidence
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then sort the parts of the argument: 'Which part of the speaker's argument is evidence, not a claim?' The answer separates the concrete proof (a statistic, example, or fact the speaker cites) from the claim it is meant to support and from the reasoning that links them.

problemArchetypes.name: Match a claim to its support
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then connect a claim to the support the speaker gives for it: 'What evidence does the speaker use to support the claim that the club needs a bigger room?' The answer names the specific reason or evidence the speaker offers for that one claim.

problemArchetypes.name: Judge whether a claim is supported or unsupported
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then evaluate one claim: 'Does the speaker support the claim that the new bus route is dangerous with evidence, or is it left unsupported?' The answer decides whether reasons and evidence back the claim and explains what is or is not provided in what the speaker said.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate the quality of the evidence
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then judge how well the support fits the claim: 'Does the evidence the speaker gives actually prove the claim, and is there enough of it?' The answer evaluates whether the speaker's evidence is relevant and sufficient, or whether it is off-topic, too thin, or merely an opinion presented as proof.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the unsupported or weak move
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then find the part of the spoken argument that lacks real support: 'Which claim does the speaker make without backing it up with reasons or evidence?' The answer identifies the assertion that rests on opinion, feeling, loaded wording, or a sweeping generalization rather than proof.

problemArchetypes.name: Separate supported claims from unsupported claims
problemArchetypes.example: Read the transcript, then divide the speaker's claims by whether they are backed up: 'Which of the speaker's claims is supported by evidence, and which is only asserted?' The answer correctly sorts a claim that has reasons and evidence behind it from one the speaker simply states.

Easy.description: A short, plainly worded transcript of a single speaker (roughly 80 to 130 words) that states one clear position and offers a small number of clearly marked claims with obvious support, embedded in the item. The task is to identify: the speaker's overall argument, one claim, or one clearly stated piece of evidence, or to decide whether a single obvious claim is supported. The answer is stated or strongly signaled on the surface of what the speaker said; little inference is required.
constraints: Stimulus is one short, single-speaker transcript (about 80 to 130 words) included in the prompt
The speaker's position and supporting evidence are stated explicitly and plainly
Identify-level task: name the argument, point to a claim, name one piece of evidence, or decide if an obvious claim is supported
The link between claim and evidence is direct; no multi-step inference needed
Familiar grade 6 contexts such as a class presentation, school announcement, or short speech

Medium.description: A moderately complex single-speaker transcript (roughly 150 to 250 words) that advances a position through two or more claims, some well supported and at least one weakly supported or unsupported, embedded in the item. The task requires analysis: match a claim to the specific reason or evidence behind it, distinguish a reason from evidence, or determine which of several claims the speaker leaves unsupported. The answer is grounded in the speaker's words but not stated word for word.
constraints: Stimulus is a longer single-speaker transcript (about 150 to 250 words) included in the prompt
Mixes supported and unsupported claims so the student must compare them
Analyze-level task: match a claim to its support, separate reason from evidence, or find which claim is unsupported
Some inference required; the strength of the speaker's support must be weighed, not just read off the surface
Contexts such as a persuasive speech, oral report, or debate turn

Hard.description: A longer or more layered spoken-argument transcript (roughly 280 to 420 words), which may be a single extended speech or a short exchange between two speakers, that builds a position through several claims, blends solid evidence with opinion, emotional appeal, or biased language, and may include a counter-point. The task requires evaluation and synthesis: trace the whole spoken argument, judge whether the overall case is well supported, evaluate the relevance and sufficiency of the speaker's evidence, or explain why a specific claim fails despite sounding persuasive. Requires sustained inference across multiple parts of the transcript.
constraints: Stimulus is a longer transcript (about 280 to 420 words), a single extended speech or a brief two-speaker exchange, included in the prompt
Builds the argument through several claims and mixes genuine evidence with opinion, appeal, or bias
Evaluate or synthesize task: trace the full argument, judge overall support, weigh relevance and sufficiency of evidence, or explain why a persuasive-sounding claim is unsupported
Requires inference that draws on what the speaker said in several places in the transcript
When two speakers are present, the item makes clear which speaker's argument is being evaluated

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the topic of the speech with the speaker's argument, naming what the speaker is talking about instead of the position the speaker takes
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that states the subject of the speech rather than the claim the speaker wants the audience to accept

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student cannot tell a claim apart from the evidence that supports it, treating a fact or statistic the speaker cites as if it were the claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a piece of the speaker's evidence (a statistic, fact, or example) and labels it as the speaker's claim, or selects a claim and calls it the evidence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes any claim the speaker makes must be supported simply because the speaker states it confidently or repeats it
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that says a claim is supported when the speaker actually offers only opinion, feeling, or repetition and no real reasons or evidence

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student counts an emotional appeal or strong, biased wording from the speaker as if it were factual evidence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Identifies a line the speaker uses to stir feeling or persuade through loaded language as the evidence that proves the claim

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student matches a claim to a true detail the speaker mentioned that does not actually support that particular claim
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a fact the speaker stated that is irrelevant to the specific claim the question asks about

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges a claim as well supported based on how long the speaker talked about it rather than the relevance or sufficiency of the evidence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that calls a claim well supported because the speaker said a lot about it, even though the evidence given does not actually prove the point

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a reason (the logic for why a claim holds) as interchangeable with evidence (the concrete proof), or vice versa
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects the speaker's stated reasoning and labels it as evidence, or labels a concrete fact the speaker cited as the reason, blurring the two

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student evaluates whether the speaker's claim is true in real life instead of whether the speaker supported it within the presentation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that judges the claim by outside knowledge or personal agreement rather than by the support the speaker actually provided
